title: Carmen 85 — Odi et amo
author: Gaius Valerius Catullus
translator_date: 1913 (Loeb Classical Library, US public domain: pre-1929)
source_notes: English translation by Francis Warre Cornish, Catullus, Tibullus, Pervigilium Veneris, Loeb Classical Library (1913), now in the US public domain.
reading_notes: Perhaps the most famous two lines in Latin poetry. Four verbs — odi, amo, fieri, excrucior — compress the whole psychology of loving what one cannot stop resenting. Note the absence of a pronoun for 'her': Catullus does not need to name her.

lines.original: Odi et amo. Quare id faciam, fortasse requiris.
lines.english: I hate and love. Why I do so, perhaps you ask?
lines.gloss: Odi = 'I hate' (perfect-for-present of ōdi, defective verb); et = 'and'; amo = 'I love' (1st sg. present); Quare = 'why'; id = 'that, it' (accusative neuter); faciam = 'I do' (present subjunctive; deliberative); fortasse = 'perhaps'; requiris = 'you ask' (2nd sg. of requiro).

lines.original: Nescio, sed fieri sentio et excrucior.
lines.english: I know not, but I feel it, and I am in torment.
lines.gloss: Nescio = 'I do not know' (ne + scio); sed = 'but'; fieri = 'to happen, be made' (passive infinitive of facio); sentio = 'I feel, perceive' (1st sg. present); et = 'and'; excrucior = 'I am tortured, crucified' (1st sg. present passive of excrucio).
